title: How archaeologists date artifacts: methods explained
seo_title: How Archaeologists Date Artifacts: Dating Methods Explained
meta_description: How archaeologists date artifacts: stratigraphy, typology, radiocarbon, thermoluminescence, OSL, tree rings, coins and inscriptions, with Indian examples.
summary: Archaeologists date artifacts in two ways. Relative dating, through stratigraphy and typology, puts finds in order from older to younger. Absolute dating gives an age in years, using radiocarbon on organic material, thermoluminescence on pottery, OSL on buried sediment, tree rings on wood, and coins or inscriptions that name rulers or eras.

sections.h2: Relative and absolute dating: two kinds of answer
paras: When an archaeologist says a pot is old, the first question is: older than what? Relative dating answers that by placing things in sequence. It does not give a number of years, but it is cheap, quick and works on almost everything found in an excavation.

Absolute dating, sometimes called chronometric dating, gives an age in calendar years, usually with a margin of error. It depends on laboratory methods or on objects that carry a date, such as an inscribed coin. Good chronology combines both: a firm sequence from the excavation, pinned to calendar years at a few points.

Stratigraphy is the foundation of archaeological dating. Soil and debris build up over time, so in an undisturbed sequence the lower layers are older than the ones above. This is the law of superposition, borrowed from geology.

Real sites are rarely that simple. People dig pits, build foundations into older levels, and rodents move small objects up and down. The excavator's job is to spot these cuts and record which layer seals which, so that a find can be assigned to the right phase. Excavation reports in India usually present this as a sequence of periods, for example Period I (Chalcolithic), Period II (early historic), and so on.

A useful idea here is the terminus post quem: the date after which a layer must have formed. If a floor contains a coin of a particular king, the floor was laid during or after his reign, however old the rest of the material looks.

Objects made by people change in style over time, much as cars or phones do today. Typology sorts artifacts into types and arranges them in sequence. Once a type has been dated at one site, it helps date similar finds elsewhere.

Pottery is the workhorse of typology in India. Ochre Coloured Pottery, Painted Grey Ware and Northern Black Polished Ware each belong to broad periods in the Ganga plains, and a trained eye can often place a sherd in its period at a glance. Stone tools, beads, terracotta figurines and architectural styles are dated the same way. A hands-on [pottery identification workshop](clay-and-the-past-a-pottery-workshop.html) is the quickest way to see how this works.

Radiocarbon (carbon-14) dating works on anything that was once alive: charcoal, seeds, bone, wood, shell. Living things take in carbon, including a small, steady proportion of radioactive carbon-14. When they die, the intake stops and the carbon-14 decays at a known rate, with a half-life of about 5,730 years. Measuring what remains gives the time since death.

The method reaches back roughly 50,000 years. Raw results must be calibrated against curves built from tree rings and other records, because the amount of carbon-14 in the atmosphere has varied. Modern laboratories use accelerator mass spectrometry (AMS), which needs only a tiny sample. In India, radiocarbon dates on charred grain and charcoal underpin the chronology of Harappan and Neolithic sites.

Minerals such as quartz and feldspar slowly store energy from natural radiation in the ground. Heating or exposure to sunlight releases that energy and resets the clock. Thermoluminescence (TL) dating measures the light given off when a sample is heated in the laboratory, and so dates the last time pottery, brick or burnt stone was fired.

Optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) measures the energy stored since sediment grains were last exposed to sunlight, which tells you when they were buried. It is widely used for river deposits, dunes and prehistoric sites well beyond the range of radiocarbon. Luminescence dates generally carry wider error margins than radiocarbon, but they reach much further back.

Trees in seasonal climates add one growth ring a year, and the pattern of thick and thin rings reflects the weather. By overlapping samples from living trees, old timbers and buried wood, researchers build long master sequences. A beam from a building can then be matched to the sequence and dated, sometimes to the exact year it was felled.

Dendrochronology is very precise but needs suitable species and long reference sequences. In South Asia its use is mostly in the Himalaya, where conifers record clear rings; elsewhere it matters chiefly as the backbone of radiocarbon calibration.

sections.h2: Coins and inscriptions: dates written by the past
paras: For the historical period, coins and inscriptions are often the best dating tools in India. Many inscriptions name a ruler, or give a date in an era such as the Vikrama, Shaka or Gupta era, which can be converted to the common calendar. Coins carry rulers' names and portraits and can be placed in sequence. Our guides to [epigraphy](what-is-epigraphy.html) and [numismatics](what-is-numismatics.html) explain how specialists read them.

A coin dates the layer it was found in only from below: it shows the layer is no older than the coin's issue, though coins could circulate for a long time. That is why archaeologists cross-check coins against pottery, stratigraphy and scientific dates. For a full classroom treatment of all these methods, our lecture on [chronology and archaeological dating](chronology-and-archaeological-dating.html) works through real Indian sequences.

faq.q: How do archaeologists know how old something is?
faq.a: They combine several lines of evidence. The layer an object came from shows whether it is older or younger than other finds. Its style can be compared with dated examples. Organic material from the same layer can be radiocarbon dated, pottery can be dated by thermoluminescence, and coins or inscriptions may name a ruler or give a date.

faq.q: How far back can carbon dating go?
faq.a: Radiocarbon dating works up to about 50,000 years. Beyond that, too little carbon-14 remains to measure reliably. For older sites, archaeologists use luminescence methods such as OSL, or other techniques based on volcanic deposits and other geological processes.

faq.q: Can carbon dating be used on stone or metal?
faq.a: No. Radiocarbon dating works only on material that was once alive, such as charcoal, wood, seeds, bone or shell. Stone tools and metal objects are dated indirectly, from organic material found in the same layer, from their style, or, for fired clay and burnt stone, by thermoluminescence.

faq.q: What is the difference between relative and absolute dating?
faq.a: Relative dating puts things in order without giving years: this layer is older than that one, this pot style came before that one. Absolute dating gives an age in calendar years, with a margin of error, through methods such as radiocarbon, luminescence, tree rings, or dated coins and inscriptions.

faq.q: Which dating method is most accurate?
faq.a: Dendrochronology can be accurate to a single year when a good reference sequence exists. A dated inscription can also be very precise. Calibrated radiocarbon dates usually give ranges of a few decades to a couple of centuries. Accuracy depends as much on a well-recorded context as on the laboratory method.

posts.hook: Carbon dating does not work on stone.
posts.caption: Radiocarbon dates only things that were once alive: charcoal, seeds, bone, wood. Stone tools are dated from the layer they lie in, or the charcoal beside them.

posts.hook: A coin in a layer tells you its minimum age, not its exact age.
posts.caption: Coins circulated for years, sometimes centuries. Archaeologists use them to say a floor is no older than the coin, then cross-check with pottery and scientific dates.
